In a Montreal apartment in 2014, Ian Goodfellow sketched an idea on a napkin that would let
one neural network critique another until both produced images no human could easily dismiss
as fake.
The goal was straightforward, give computers the ability to imagine new examples of faces,
faces, objects, and scenes, without needing millions of labeled photographs.
Within five years, the identical architecture was being used to map one person's face onto
another's body in video, creating the first wave of widely circulated deep fake pornography
and political fabrications.
Ian Goodfellow was a PhD student at the University of Montreal, working under Yoshua Benjyo when
he proposed generative adversarial networks.
At the time, generative models such as variational auto encoders produce blurry or
low-resolution outputs that fail to capture fine detail.
Goodfellow's insight was to pit two networks against each other, a generator that creates
images and a discriminator that tries to tell real images from generated ones.
The competition he argued would force the generator to improve until its outputs became
statistically indistinguishable from reality.
The paper, generative adversarial nets, was submitted in June 2014 and presented at the
Neural Information Processing Systems Conference that December.
Researchers saw immediate promise for data augmentation, medical imaging simulation, and creative
tools.
No one in the room that day discussed video manipulation or non-consensual content.
The conversation centered on unsupervised learning and the longstanding difficulty of modeling
complex distributions.
The 2014 paper spread quickly through the academic community.
By 2015, follow-up work at Facebook, AI Research, and Google Brain demonstrated GAN's generating
recognizable bedroom scenes and human faces at 64 by 64 resolution.
In 2016, Nvidia's progressive GAN's paper pushed output quality to 1,024 by 1,024, making
celebrity-style face synthesis feasible.
Early adopters celebrated the results in conference talks and open source repositories on GitHub.
A small number of researchers noted that the same fidelity that made the images impressive
could also make them deceptive, but these cautions appeared mainly in footnotes rather than
press releases.
The first public demonstration of face swapping video arrived in late 2017 on Reddit, where
a user released code that combined GAN-based face generation with traditional computer vision
tracking.
The Reddit post titled Deep Fakes received over 100,000 views in its first week and spawned
a dedicated subreddit that reached 100,000 subscribers within months.
The software required only a few hours of source footage and modest consumer GPUs, lowering
the barrier from professional studios to individual users.
By early 2018, the same technique had been used to insert the faces of female celebrities
into pornographic videos.
One widely shared compilation reportedly accumulated tens of millions of views before platform
takedowns.
Political applications followed in April 2018, a video of Barack Obama appeared to call Donald
Trump a complete dipshit, created by comedian Jordan Piel and BuzzFeed to illustrate the risk.
The causal mechanism was direct.
The adversarial training loop rewarded any improvement in visual realism, exactly the
property needed to defeat casual human inspection.
Second order effects emerged quickly.
Newsrooms began questioning the reliability of video evidence, while dating app companies
reported users demanding live verification calls to confirm identities.
By 2019, estimates from deep trace labs suggested more than 96% of online deep fake videos
were non-concentral pornography, the overwhelming majority targeting women.
Detection tools developed in response created an arms race.
Each new detector trained on existing fakes simply taught the next generation of generators how
to evade it. Major platforms responded with policy changes.
Reddit banned deep fake pornography in February 2018, Twitter and porn hub followed with similar
prohibitions. The US Congress held hearings in 2019, and several states passed laws criminalizing
non-concentral deep fake pornography. At the same time, the underlying research continued
under new names, style-gan, big-gan and later diffusion models, because the scientific value remained
clear. Some labs adopted responsible release practices, such as watermarking or limiting training data,
yet enforcement proved difficult once code was public. Today, consumer apps can produce
convincing face swaps and seconds on smartphones, and detection remains unreliable against high-quality
outputs. The original GAN architecture has been largely superseded by newer generative methods,
yet the core tension it introduced, easy synthesis of realistic media, persists.
Open research into generative systems will continue to produce dual use capabilities.
The same objective function that improves medical image simulation also improves
undetectable fakes. Institutions that fund or publish such work therefore need pre-publication
review processes that consider misuse pathways beyond the author's original intent.
Finally, once a generative technique reaches consumer hardware, retroactive controls become largely
symbolic. The relevant question for any new generative model today is not whether it can be misused,
but how quickly that misuse will outrun the safeguards built around it. That's unintended consequences
for today. If this episode gave you something to think about, share it with a friend who'd appreciate
the story. Subscribe wherever you listen, and we'll be back tomorrow with another case.
